title: Kaliya
carry: spared, and sent to the ocean

segments.voice: Yesterday the boy danced on Kaliya's hoods until the serpent's pride was gone, and Kaliya remembered the Lord. Your line was the dance on the hoods.

The serpent is beaten. He lies broken in the water, the boy still standing on his heads. And out of the pool come the serpent's wives. The Bhagavata calls them the naga wives, and they don't come to fight. They come with their children in front of them, hair loose, clothes disordered, and bow before Krishna with their palms joined. Kaliya can't speak for himself anymore. So they speak for him.
screen: `THE SERPENT IS BEATEN.` → `HIS WIVES COME OUT OF THE POOL.` → `THEY SPEAK FOR HIM.`

segments.voice: What they say is surprising. They don't argue that their husband is innocent. They call his punishment fair, more than fair: a grace. Your feet have touched his head, they say, and others perform long austerities hoping for the dust of those feet. Then they ask one thing: spare him. He is our husband. Let him live. And Krishna lets him go. Kaliya, slowly getting his breath back, speaks plainly. We serpents are born this way, angry by nature, with poison in us. It's hard to let go of what you're made of. Krishna doesn't lecture him. He gives him a way forward: leave this pool, go to the ocean with your family, so the river can be clean again for the people and the cows. Then Krishna names the fear that brought Kaliya here. He was hiding. Garuda, the eagle who preys on serpents, could not enter this pool because of a sage's old curse, so this poisoned corner of the Yamuna was the one place he felt safe. And Krishna answers that fear. Garuda won't harm you now, he says, because you carry the marks of my feet on your hoods. So the story ends without anyone destroyed. The poison leaves the river. The serpent leaves with his family, his fear answered. And the feet that broke his pride become the thing that protects him.
screen: `"YOUR FEET HAVE TOUCHED HIS HEAD."` · `"WE ARE BORN THIS WAY."` · `GO TO THE OCEAN; LET THE RIVER BE CLEAN.` · then, large: `THE FOOTPRINTS PROTECT HIM.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone whose sharpness you've felt, and gently wonder: what might they be afraid of, what corner did they crawl into to feel safe? You don't have to excuse anything; just let the question soften the picture as you breathe, and, if you can, wish them somewhere better to live than their poison. If you pray, you can hold them in your prayer.
Kaliya. The serpent spared at his wives' plea, sent to the ocean, and protected by the very footprints that subdued him.
Your line: spared, and sent to the ocean. Tomorrow, a boy asks his father a question. Day eight hundred ninety-four, done.

howItsDone: Devotees retell the prayer of Kaliya's wives as a model of surrender, and in some depictions of Kaliya-mardana the naga wives are shown with joined palms beside the serpent.
